stem: A 3-week-old boy has blisters on his hands and feet and where the diaper rubs, always at sites of friction. The blisters heal without scarring, nails are normal, and the mouth is spared. A biopsy shows a split through the basal keratinocytes.
oneliner: 3-week-old M + friction blisters on hands, feet and diaper area + heals without scar + split through basal keratinocytes → which protein is defective?
ask: Which protein is most likely defective?

whyNot.A: Defective anchoring fibrils give **dystrophic EB**: a **split below the basement membrane**, scarring and milia; his blisters heal **without scar**
whyNot.B: Defective laminin-332 causes **junctional EB**, with a split in the **lamina lucida** and severe mucosal disease
whyNot.C: This desmosomal protein is attacked in **pemphigus vulgaris**, an **acquired** autoimmune disease with a **suprabasal** cleft, not a split through basal cells in a newborn
whyNot.D: Mutations cause **Marfan syndrome** (tall stature, lens dislocation, aortic dilatation), not blistering

why: **Keratin 5 and 14** form the cytoskeleton of **basal keratinocytes**. When mutated, the cells rupture with minor friction, so blisters form **within the epidermis** and heal **without scar** in **epidermolysis bullosa simplex**.

idea.rule: The depth of the EB split follows the protein: keratin (inside epidermis), laminin (lamina lucida), collagen VII (below the lamina densa).
also: EB simplex: keratin 5 or 14, autosomal dominant, heals without scar
Dystrophic EB: COL7A1, scarring and milia, squamous cell carcinoma risk
Pemphigus is acquired autoimmune desmoglein disease, not an inherited keratin defect

stem: A 6-year-old girl has vaginal bleeding and early breast development. She recently fractured her leg after minor trauma, and she has a large, jagged-edged tan patch across one side of her back. X-ray shows a ground-glass lesion in the femur.
oneliner: 6F + vaginal bleeding and breast development + low-trauma leg fracture + large jagged tan patch on one side + bone lesion → which gene is mutated?
ask: Which gene is most likely mutated?

whyNot.A: Gives **smaller, smooth-bordered café-au-lait spots**, axillary freckling, neurofibromas and Lisch nodules, without **fibrous dysplasia** and precocious puberty
whyNot.C: Causes **tuberous sclerosis** with ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, seizures and renal angiomyolipomas; there are no **fractures or early puberty**
whyNot.D: An activating mutation gives **achondroplasia** (short limbs, normal trunk), not **skin patches and early puberty**
whyNot.E: Gives **MEN 2A/2B** and Hirschsprung disease, with medullary thyroid cancer, not **precocious puberty with fibrous dysplasia**

why: **Café-au-lait patch with a jagged border, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and precocious puberty** make **McCune-Albright syndrome**. A **postzygotic activating mutation of GNAS** (Gs-alpha) keeps cAMP high in affected tissues, which is why only mosaic patches are involved and hormone-making glands act autonomously.

idea.rule: Constitutively active Gs-alpha drives cAMP-dependent tissues on their own: bone, melanocytes and endocrine glands.
also: Precocious puberty from autonomous ovarian estrogen
Hyperthyroidism, growth-hormone excess and Cushing syndrome can occur
Mosaic distribution: lethal if present in every cell
Activating GNAS mutations in pituitary somatotrophs (gsp oncogene) cause acromegaly
